The old pumping station on the east bank of the river was decommissioned in 1974, and for nearly twenty years the district council argued about what to do with it. Weeds grew through the iron grating, pigeons nested in the chimney, and the building itself slowly filled with damp and rust. A developer offered to buy the site and turn the engine hall into flats, but the planning committee rejected the scheme after a long public inquiry, and a voluntary trust was allowed to purchase the site for a nominal sum.

The trust raised money from a heritage fund and spent three summers replacing the roof, repainting the cast-iron beams in the colours recorded in an 1892 photograph, and clearing the silt from the culvert that runs under the yard. Volunteers now open the doors on the first Sunday of every month, and school parties come by bus to watch the great beam engine turn. The guide, a retired fitter named Arthur Penrose, explains how the pumps lifted water from the river into a reservoir on the hill behind the town, and he is fond of pointing out that the machinery was built to run for a century and that most of the parts are still original.

The trust has also collected a small archive: ledgers, wage books, photographs and a bundle of letters written by the engineer who supervised the original installation. The letters describe the difficulty of casting the cylinder in a foundry that had attempted work of that size before, and they complain, in a formal Victorian hand, about the price of coal and the habits of the apprentices. Visitors often linger over them; a paragraph about a burst pipe in the winter of 1881 has been known to hold a reader's attention for ten minutes.

Behind the engine hall is a workshop where volunteers restore tools and demonstrate them at weekend fairs. On a bench near the window sits a lathe built in Leeds in 1911, still capable of turning a brass fitting to within a thousandth of an inch. Next to it is a collection of hand tools arranged by trade: files, chisels, planes, hammers, and a row of wooden mallets worn smooth by use. The workshop smells of oil and sawdust, and the floor is swept every evening before the doors are locked.

The trust's finances are modest. Ticket sales cover the electricity bill, a grant from the county pays the insurance, and the rest comes from a second-hand book sale held each spring in the engine hall. Last year the sale raised enough to repair the staircase to the gallery, which had been closed since a surveyor found a crack in one of the stringers in 2016.

Never in the trust's history had the annual meeting been so crowded as the one held last March, when the volunteers gathered to argue about the future of the site. Some members wanted to open a cafe in the workshop; others insisted that the building should remain a working museum and that no part of the collection should be sold to pay for the roof. After two hours of debate the trustees agreed to a compromise: the workshop would keep its tools, the book sale would continue, and the cafe would be limited to a counter in the entrance hall. Nobody left the meeting entirely satisfied, and that, Arthur said afterwards, was probably the best outcome the trust could expect.

The station opens again in April, and the volunteers will carry on without much money and without any fuss, as they have for thirty years.
